name: PT Jakarta Setiabudi Internasional Tbk

frontmatter.title: Jakarta Setiabudi: premium Bali and Jakarta hotels priced for decline
frontmatter.summary: JSPT owns eleven hotels, a large residential land bank and prime Jakarta office and retail space, yet trades at a mid-single-digit EV/EBITDA after a speculative bubble collapsed. The operating business is growing, net debt is small and the shares discount a permanent shrinkage. We initiate at BUY on fundamental value, haircut for float and governance.
thesis: The hotel division, which earns the large majority of group profit, is priced by the market as if the post-bubble share price, not the cash flow, were the truth.
Nine-month revenue is up strongly on hotel pricing and a real-estate land sale; we treat the land sale as lumpy rather than recurring and still find the equity undervalued.
Net debt is small against a large cash balance, so the equity is geared to operating cash flow rather than to refinancing risk.
The variant view is a governance and float discount, not an earnings problem: the controlling family owns the large majority and the free float is thin, which is why the multiple is where it is.
The ways to lose money are a Bali demand shock, a related-party extraction event, or a market that keeps ignoring cash flow because the float never widens.

catalysts.event: Full-year FY2026 results and the FY2027 dividend proposal, the first clean read on post-bubble earnings power
Annual general meeting and dividend approval, the test of whether the payout ratchet continues
Residential land-bank sales and hotel revenue disclosures in the quarterly LK

blocks.text: **Rating BUY, twelve-month target Rp2,583, total return 105.9%.** The shares trade at Rp1,275, having fallen from a Rp4,220 high inside the last twelve months [S0]. We value the equity on the cash the assets produce, apply the house liquidity discount of 30.0%, and still arrive at a value more than double the market price.

This is not a distressed asset. The company owns and operates a hotel portfolio of 2,686 rooms, largely in Bali and Jakarta, a residential division with 788.4 hectares of land, 48,804 square metres of retail and 55,081 square metres of office space [S2]. In the first nine months of 2026 it reported revenue of IDR2,171.8bn, with hotel revenue of IDR1,651.4bn and real-estate revenue of IDR299.3bn [S4]. The hotel division earned about four-fifths of group profit in FY2025, when group revenue was IDR2,417.2bn, EBITDA IDR853.1bn and net profit attributable to shareholders IDR298.1bn [S2].

The market is not disputing those numbers; it is refusing to pay for them. At Rp1,275 on 2,319m shares the whole equity is capitalised at IDR2,956.4bn, a fraction of the assets it owns, and after the cash and debt on the September 2026 balance sheet the enterprise value is a low multiple of EBITDA [S0]. Our reverse DCF — the engine's own DCF, run backwards on the same WACC and forecast horizon to solve for the revenue growth rate that equates the modelled value to the price — says today's price implies revenue shrinking at -6.4% a year in perpetuity. Nothing in the operating record supports that: hotel revenue rose from IDR1,485.0bn in the nine months to September 2025 to IDR1,651.4bn in the same nine months of 2026, a double-digit rate, and the Bali resorts ran above 85.0% occupancy through the second half of 2025 [S2][S4].

The variant view is therefore about why the discount exists, not whether the earnings are real. Three things explain it. First, the stock was a speculative vehicle: it rose roughly tenfold in late 2024, was suspended for a day in January 2025, then gave almost all of it back [S2]. Second, control is concentrated: the controlling shareholder and affiliates hold the large majority of the shares and the free float is 8.3%, so the tape is thin and stays thin [S0][S2]. Third, the group borrows from related parties and leases land from its parent, so a minority holder is structurally a price-taker in the family's capital allocation [S3]. We take those seriously: they are why we apply a full liquidity haircut to a DCF value that already treats the land bank conservatively. The float is not the input that sets that haircut — the whole discount is the fund's liquidity ladder applied to a three-month average daily traded value of IDR46.1m; the float tells us why the tape is that thin and why it may stay thin [S0].

What moves the value, in order: the Bali and Jakarta hotel EBITDA line, which is the majority of profit; the pace at which the residential land bank is monetised; and the discount rate the market applies to a controlled, thinly traded company. The first two are observable every quarter. The third is a re-rating we do not assume.

JSPT is the listed property and hospitality arm of the Darmadi family's Jakarta Setiabudi group. It is not a hotel operator in the managerial sense: it owns the bricks, the land, the buildings and the rooms, and contracts international brands and managers to run several of the flagships. The portfolio description in the annual report is precise: the hotel division holds 11 hotels with 2,686 rooms; the residential division manages 788.4 hectares of land; the retail division has 5 properties with 48,804 square metres of lettable area; and the office division manages 55,081 square metres [S2]. The data pack counts 493 employees, while the annual report states 1,932; we use the filing's number [S2][S0].

The estate spans the top and the middle of the market. At the top sit the Grand Hyatt Bali and Andaz Bali in Nusa Dua and Sanur, the Hyatt Regency in Yogyakarta and the Mercure Convention Center in Jakarta. Below them sit the economy brands: Ibis Budget in Menteng and Cikini, and POP! hotels in Kemang, Malioboro, Semarang and elsewhere [S2]. That barbell is deliberate. The luxury resorts carry the average daily rate and the international tour-operator relationships; the budget city hotels carry occupancy and a domestic demand base that is less cyclical than inbound tourism.

Revenue is reported in four operating divisions, and the mix matters more than the headline. In FY2025 the hotel division produced IDR1,988.5bn of the IDR2,417.2bn group total, the office division about a twentieth, the retail division a little more, and the residential division a little more again [S2]. Within the hotel line, the FY2025 contract-revenue note splits room revenue, food and beverage, and ancillary facilities, with rooms the largest single component [S2]. The profit mix is even more concentrated than the revenue mix: the annual report attributes the large majority of group profit to the hotel division, with the residential, office and retail divisions each contributing a single-digit share [S2].

That concentration is the analytical starting point. JSPT is, for valuation purposes, a Bali and Jakarta hotel owner with a property-development option attached. The office and retail portfolios are long-lease annuities with high occupancy in the company's own buildings and modest mark-to-market; the residential land bank is a real option whose timing the family controls [S2]. The hotel business, by contrast, is a daily-priced operating business exposed to airlift, visa policy and the rupiah.

The group structure is a holding company over operating subsidiaries. PT Jan Darmadi Investindo owns 51% directly, with the rest held by other shareholders including affiliated vehicles [S2]. The company has been listed since 1998 and its paid-up capital is small relative to the asset base [S2]. The subsidiaries carry the assets and, importantly, the minority partners: the Bali hotel vehicles and the Copylas entity have minority shareholders, and the consolidated balance sheet carries a large minority interest that absorbs a meaningful share of group profit [S0][S3]. A buyer of JSPT equity is buying the parent's share of those subsidiaries, not the whole consolidated cash flow.

Strategy as disclosed is unremarkable and, for our purposes, credible. Management talks about revenue quality over occupancy volume, rate discipline, selective technology investment and asset reliability, and about monetising residential land in tranches rather than dumping it [S2]. There is no announced mega-project, no rights issue and no debt-funded expansion. The annual report confirms no corporate stock action in 2025, no split, bonus shares or convertibles [S2]. That matters after a year in which the share price moved by an order of magnitude on no corporate action at all.

Indonesian hospitality groups of this type typically sit inside family conglomerates that own the land through separate vehicles and lease it to the listed operating company. That structure is legal and common, but it means the listed entity economics depend on lease terms set with a related party rather than on market rents, and asset-sale decisions are made at family level, leaving minority holders limited ability to force a sale or a payout.

The demand side is Indonesian tourism and domestic corporate travel. The annual report puts hospitality at just under four per cent of GDP, cites a national hotel occupancy rate of 49.3% from the statistical agency, and notes that the residential segment remained the largest part of the property market while the office segment recovered to 75.8% occupancy and retail malls held around 74% [S2]. Those are national and Jakarta numbers; the company's own Bali resorts operate in a structurally tighter market, where management reports occupancy above 85.0% in the second half of 2025 [S2]. The gap between that national average and a mid-eighties Bali resort occupancy is the investment case in one statistic: the company owns the scarce end of the market.

For 2026 management expects a more disciplined industry, with growth coming from average daily rate rather than from filling more rooms, and describes rate increases as evidence that hotels can hold price without discounting to buy occupancy [S2]. That is the right operating posture for an owner of irreplaceable beachfront and central-business-district land, and it is corroborated by the first nine months of 2026. The segment note prints the 2025 comparative alongside the current column: hotel revenue of IDR1,651.4bn against IDR1,485.0bn in the same nine months of last year, with the residential division adding IDR299.3bn from land and building sales against IDR113.7bn a year earlier, the difference being the lumpy land transaction rather than a change in operating run-rate [S4].

Competitive position is asset-based, not brand-based. JSPT does not own the Hyatt or Accor brands; it owns the sites and the buildings and pays management and franchise fees for the flags. The operating expense note shows management fees as one of the larger cost lines [S2]. The moat is location and land title, not customer loyalty: a competitor cannot build another Nusa Dua beachfront or another Sudirman office tower, but a competitor can and does open new hotels in Canggu, Ubud and Seminyak, and can take share in the budget segment where the POP! and Ibis properties compete. On a five-forces reading, rivalry is high and rising in the mid-market, supplier power is moderate through the brands and tour operators, buyer power is high in corporate and MICE segments, substitutes are plentiful in villas, apartments and online travel agencies, and new entry is constrained only where land is constrained.

The office and retail divisions face a different structure. Jakarta central-business-district office occupancy in the mid-seventies with limited new supply is a recovering market, not a tight one, and the annual report's own discussion of hybrid work and flight-to-quality suggests the spread between Grade A and Grade B will keep widening [S2]. Retail is a tenant-mix business, and the company's commentary is candid that premium and upper-middle malls are outperforming the rest [S2]. Both divisions are effectively bond-like: contracted rents, renegotiated on rolling leases, with occupancy risk at renewal.

Regulation touches the business in three places. Hotels are subject to the regional hotel tax rather than VAT, which is why the group's effective tax rate differs from the statutory rate, and the annual report discloses final-tax treatment on part of its income [S2]. Land is held under right-to-build and right-to-manage titles, with the Grand Hyatt Bali site sitting on a lease from the Bali tourism development corporation that carries a minimum lease compensation obligation [S2]. And inbound tourism depends on visa and airlift policy, which is outside the company's control and outside our forecast.

The macro deck gives us the rupiah and the domestic cycle: the dollar is expected at 18,350 and the policy rate at 5.8% [S0]. A weaker rupiah helps inbound tourism receipts in rupiah terms and hurts the dollar cost of imported food, beverage and fittings. The company also carries dollar-denominated related-party debt, so a weaker rupiah raises the rupiah cost of that debt [S3]. On balance we treat the rupiah as second-order for EBITDA and first-order for the translation of dollar debt.

The house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with an explicit AVOID tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive property and consumer discretionary, and JSPT screens as both [S0]. We keep the name, and the reason is sourced rather than a preference. Its revenue is earned from foreign guests and its costs are largely rupiah, so a weaker rupiah is a tailwind to inbound receipts rather than a margin squeeze [S2]. Its net debt is small enough that the rate cycle does not reach the equity, and the debt it does carry is mostly fixed-rate bank term loans and leases rather than floating working-capital lines [S3]. What the tilt does change is the shape and the rate of our forecast. It is one reason we hold terminal growth low and assume no re-rating of the multiple, so the AVOID view is expressed in the fade rather than in an optimistic volume path; it is also one reason we have not cut the cost of equity to the bottom of the house band — our rate sits above it, and the valuation section sets out what that does to the target in both directions.

Bali tourism has historically been resilient to Indonesian domestic shocks but highly exposed to global travel cycles and to airlift from Australia, China and Europe. Resort owners with long land leases and dollar-linked management contracts typically see rate fall faster than occupancy in a downturn, because operators discount to protect volume. That asymmetry is why hotel EBITDA is more cyclical than hotel revenue.

The history is one of recovery followed by a plateau. Group revenue rose from IDR1,376.6bn in FY2022 to IDR2,417.2bn in FY2025, but almost all of that growth happened by FY2024; FY2025 was essentially flat at the top line [S0]. EBITDA followed the same path, from IDR504.0bn to IDR844.5bn, and slipped in FY2025 as costs grew faster than revenue [S0][S2]. Net profit attributable to shareholders nevertheless rose to IDR298.1bn because the interest bill fell and was better covered [S0]. Reported earnings per share were Rp129 [S0].

The first nine months of 2026 break the plateau. Revenue of IDR2,171.8bn is well ahead of the comparable period, driven by two distinct engines: hotel revenue of IDR1,651.4bn, reflecting rate and occupancy in Bali plus a stronger Jakarta corporate calendar, and real-estate revenue of IDR299.3bn from land and building sales [S4]. The real-estate line needs care. It is transaction-driven rather than contracted: the half-year total of IDR275.6bn is recognised on transfer of land and buildings and the segment note carries it at a gross margin far above the hotel business [S3]. A land sale is not an annuity, so we model the real-estate division as a lumpy series that reverts toward the FY2025 run rate rather than extrapolating the first-half spike, and we take no view on the identity or repeat behaviour of any single counterparty because the statements do not disclose one.

Our forecast is deliberately mechanical. FY2026E revenue is IDR2,828.1bn, growth of 17.0%, which requires only a modest fourth quarter after nine months of IDR2,171.8bn [S4]. Growth fades to 6.0% in FY2027E and to 4.5% by FY2030E. Two sourced things drive the fade. First, FY2026E carries the land sale and the following years do not repeat it, so the base effect alone accounts for most of the step down. Second, hotel rate growth is assumed to normalise toward the supply-driven market described in the industry section: management's own account has competitors opening in Canggu, Ubud and Seminyak and taking share in the budget segment where POP! and Ibis compete [S2]. What we do not assume is a collapse: the bull case holds hotel revenue at the first-half growth rate for two more years, because rooms are fixed and incremental rate falls almost entirely to EBITDA [S3]. We assume no new hotel, no new tower and no acceleration in the land programme, because none is announced [S2].

Margins are the part of the model most likely to be argued with. The gross margin was 68.2% in FY2025 and is forecast at 70.5% for FY2026E, reflecting the high-margin land sale in the first half; it then eases toward 68.0% as the mix returns to hotel-led revenue [S0]. Total operating expenses, which in this company include depreciation exactly as the notes present them, ran at IDR1,037.4bn in FY2025 on a 68.2% gross margin [S2]. We do not model a cost cut: absolute opex is grown in line with inflation against revenue growth of 17.0% in FY2026E, so the ratio falls mechanically to 39.1% and then only slowly to 38.5% by FY2030E. That is above the nine-month run-rate, not below it. The nine-month accounts show group profit from operations of IDR737.3bn and operating expenses carry depreciation and amortisation of IDR177.3bn [S4]; adding the charge back puts nine-month EBITDA at a margin above the 41.1% we forecast for the full year. The resulting EBITDA margin is 41.1% in FY2026E against 34.9% in FY2025, and the step is the land sale plus the fixed cost base, not an operating-leverage assumption. If we held the FY2025 ratio instead, FY2026E EBITDA and the target would both be lower; we show that direction rather than claim the ratio is conservative.

Depreciation is the line that most often distorts Indonesian property accounts, because the direct-method cash-flow statement in the data pack can carry a fraction of the real charge. Here it does not: the notes show depreciation and amortisation of IDR234.6bn in FY2025, matching the data pack's IDR234.6bn, so the history needs no restatement and EBITDA is not flattered [S2][S0]. The segment note splits that charge mostly to the hotel division, with office and retail sharing the rest [S2].

Cash generation is strong. Operating cash flow covered capex of IDR90.4bn on revenue of IDR2,417.2bn in FY2025, and free cash flow covered the dividend several times over [S0]. We forecast capex at 5.0% of revenue, above the recent historical rate because the Bali rooms need a rolling soft-refurbishment cycle; even so the business throws off cash [S0]. Working capital is negative, as a hotel and landlord should be, since room deposits, tenant security deposits and advances on land sales fund the business, and we hold it at -7.0% of revenue [S0][S3].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case. At 31 December 2025 the group held IDR1,745.4bn of cash against IDR2,491.4bn of debt, leaving net debt of IDR746.0bn, or 0.9x EBITDA [S0]. Leverage has fallen since. The June 2026 half-year statements show bank loans of IDR2,011.3bn against IDR2,011.4bn of time deposits within cash and cash equivalents [S3], and the valuation bridge uses the later, 30 September 2026 balance sheet from the nine-month accounts, on which net debt is a fraction of forecast EBITDA [S4][S0]. The debt is bank term loans and lease liabilities, with the lease book tied to land under the Bali hotels; part of the bank debt is dollar-denominated [S3]. Interest cover is comfortable, and the loan covenants require bank notice before a dividend, which is a constraint worth knowing rather than a problem today [S3]. Minorities hold a large share of equity, so consolidated net debt overstates the parent's leverage and consolidated EBITDA overstates the parent's claim; our valuation bridges both. The forecast then rolls the other way: free cash flow to equity exceeds a payout of 20.0%, no new borrowing is assumed, and the debt line rises only through the rupiah translation of the dollar-denominated related-party loans at the macro deck's exchange rate, so the group builds cash of IDR9,595.7bn against debt of IDR2,491.4bn by FY2035E [S0][S3]. None of that terminal cash is credited in the valuation, because the equity bridge is struck on the September 2026 balance sheet and the DCF already capitalises the cash flows that build the balance — the two do not double-count.

Capital allocation is conservative: a dividend that has risen from nothing to a modest payout, capex below depreciation, and no acquisitions [S0][S2]. The payout ratio is 19.4% and the trailing dividend yield at the current price is 2.0% [S0]. That is not a dividend story, but it is evidence that cash is returned rather than recycled into the family's other vehicles.

Earnings quality gets its own paragraph, and we run the house screens on it. The accruals picture is clean: net profit sits well below operating cash flow in every year of the history, so earnings are not outrunning cash [S0]. Receivables are small relative to revenue and fell in FY2025, consistent with a cash hotel business [S2]. The two flags we carry are disclosure flags, not manipulation flags. The first is revenue mix: the real-estate line is transaction-driven and carries a gross margin well above the hotel business, so consolidated margin and consolidated growth are not repeatable and a reader should not capitalise them [S3]. We checked the customer-concentration disclosure and found none — the only concentration language in the group accounts is the boilerplate credit-risk note — so we make no concentration claim [S3][S4]. The second is related-party gravity: the group leases land from its parent, borrows from the parent and a related investment vehicle, and earns a small amount of revenue from the parent [S3]. Neither is evidence of fabrication. Both mean the consolidated numbers should be read as a family-controlled pool of cash flows rather than a set of arm's-length contracts.

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method and market multiples as cross-checks, which is the house method set for this industry and the right one for an asset-heavy owner. DCF suits JSPT because the assets are long-lived, the depreciation charge is real and large, the capital structure is stable and earnings are distorted by land-sale timing and minority interests; a P/E on a lumpy real-estate year would be meaningless. We weight DCF at 65.0% of the blend, EV/EBITDA at 25.0% and P/E at 10.0%. The DCF carries more than the house default because a land-sale year makes a P/E almost meaningless here, and the P/E carries less because the earnings it multiplies are consolidated — they include the minority partners' share of the Bali hotel profits, which the parent shareholder never receives [S0][S3].

The cost of capital build is pinned by house convention. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%; the unlevered beta of 0.9x is the industry default, levered to 1.4x at the engine's gross debt-to-equity of 0.7, giving a cost of equity of 15.3% [S0]. That is above the house cost-of-equity band for rupiah assets. We set out where it lands in both directions rather than presenting it as either caution or aggression.

The COE reaches the target through two channels that pull opposite ways. The first is the discount rate: the engine weights the COE at 57.8% of the WACC, and the DCF discounted at that WACC carries 65.0% of the blended value, so the COE is the largest single influence on the operating value. The second is the twelve-month roll, where the base value is grown at the COE of 15.3% less the forecast dividend. A higher COE pushes the first channel down and the second channel up.

The discount-rate channel dominates, and by enough to settle the direction of the net effect. An in-band COE would lower the WACC by more than the lower roll rate would take off the target, so the target would be HIGHER than the one we publish, not lower. Every increment above the band costs the target value through the discount rate; our out-of-band COE is therefore a conservative input in net terms, and no part of the bridge is stretched in our favour by it. What the paragraph cannot do is describe the roll as the only place the rate bites, or tell a reader to haircut the target for a rate that already understates it.

We keep the rate above the band rather than forcing it into it because the relevering convention, not a judgement about this company, produces it. The engine relevers at gross debt over market capitalisation, while this company holds time deposits that match its bank loans almost exactly [S3]; on a net-debt base the debt-to-equity is small, the levered beta lands on the unlevered 0.9x, and the COE is the risk-free rate plus one beta of the mature premium plus the country premium — still above the top of the band, but by a narrower margin, so the convention explains part of the gap and not all of it. The band itself is a cost-of-equity band, not a WACC band: the WACC of 11.9% sits inside it only because the after-tax cost of debt is well below the equity rate, and the two should not be compared directly. We have not added a company-specific premium for governance: we take that risk through the liquidity discount on the final target, so the reader can see operating value and control discount separately.

The DCF produces Rp3,639 per share, with terminal value at 42.7% of the total and an implied enterprise value of IDR9,456.8bn. That enterprise value is the engine's bridge output, not a market figure: the DCF equity value plus the net debt and minorities on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, less associates [S4][S3]. The conventions behind the terminal share are worth stating because they move it by a few points. Forecast cash flows are discounted at the mid-point of each fiscal year, counted from the balance-sheet date so the stub quarter is not double-counted, and terminal value is a growing perpetuity struck off the final forecast year and discounted from that year's end to the valuation date; terminal net debt does not enter the equity bridge, which is struck only on the September 2026 balance sheet [S4][S0]. Under that convention the terminal share is moderate for a property company, but the multiple-survival test is the one that matters. We run it explicitly: terminal growth is set at 2.0% so that the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA close to the peer-median multiple of 6.9x rather than multiples above it. The exit buyer therefore pays the same EV/EBITDA as the peer set, against the 3.4x the market pays for the shares today. Since the current price is distressed rather than the terminal multiple being heroic, the DCF requires a normalisation to the peer median by the terminal year — a de-rating from today's collapse, not expansion beyond the peer set. Terminal growth is also the right economic rate for the asset: capex runs below depreciation, no new hotel or tower is announced, and the land bank is finite [S2].

The cross-checks sit below the DCF and we are explicit about why and on what base year. Both legs are struck on FY2025A consolidated figures, not on the FY2026E forecast the DCF uses: EV/EBITDA at the peer median of 6.9x times FY2025A EBITDA gives Rp2,073, and P/E at 19.1x times FY2025A parent earnings gives Rp2,451 [S0]. FY2025 is the last audited year and, unlike FY2026E, carries no land sale, so the multiple legs are the more conservative base. Neither is a like-for-like comparison: the listed leisure peer set is dominated by distressed Bali villa developers with different asset quality and leverage, and the multiple legs are struck on consolidated figures that include the minority partners' share of EBITDA and earnings [S0]. We keep them at a combined weight of a third because they are the market's own language, but we do not let them anchor the target.

Nothing in that blend pays for the land bank or the buildings as assets. As a cross-check rather than a valuation leg, the segment note carries the office and retail divisions' segment assets at IDR361.0bn and IDR450.7bn respectively [S4], against a whole listed equity of 2,319m shares at Rp1,275 [S0], before ascribing any value to the residential land or the hotels. That is a floor on what the estate would fetch in a sale at book, and it is the mechanism the bull case uses: the office and retail asset sale at segment-note book value is one of the three bull drivers, alongside faster land monetisation and hotel revenue held at the first-half growth rate [S4].

The inputs below the last actual are deliberate and each is sourced. Operating expenses at 39.1% of revenue are above the nine-month run-rate implied by the segment note [S4]. Capex at 5.0% of revenue is above the FY2025 actual of IDR90.4bn on IDR2,417.2bn of revenue [S0]. Both multiple legs are struck on the more conservative FY2025A base rather than FY2026E [S0]. No value is ascribed to the land bank or to the office and retail assets outside the DCF, and the liquidity discount is applied in full [S0][S4]. The one input that runs the other way is tax: 24.0% against the FY2025 effective rate, and it is justified by the nine-month charge of IDR89.3bn on IDR486.5bn of profit for the period, which is lower again because of final tax on the land sale [S4]. The net effect of the stack is to understate the target if the nine-month run-rate holds, and we say so rather than present it as neutral.

The blended value is Rp3,690 before the liquidity adjustment, which is the engine's output from the legs above rather than a market figure. We then apply the house liquidity discount of 30.0% for a stock with a 8.3% free float, a controlling shareholder with the large majority of the shares and a trading suspension inside the last two years; the discount itself is the fund's ladder applied to three-month traded value of IDR46.1m, not a float penalty [S0][S2]. That gives a twelve-month target of Rp2,583 and a total return including the forecast dividend of 105.9% [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows what matters. A one-point move in the terminal growth rate or the cost of capital swings the value by more than a change in near-term revenue growth, which is typical of a long-duration asset and is why the discount rate is the first place a reader should look rather than the last — and why we have not cut it to the bottom of the house band. The two assumptions carrying most of the value are the hotel EBITDA margin after the land sale normalises and the terminal growth rate; a change in either moves the target by more than a change in the FY2027 growth rate. Because the value is sensitive to the rate, and because the rate we use is above the band rather than below it, the error in the published target from the discount rate runs in the conservative direction.

What does today's price imply? Running the engine's DCF backwards at the same WACC and over the same forecast horizon — solving for the single revenue growth rate applied from FY2027E that makes the modelled value equal Rp1,275 — implies revenue declining at -6.4% a year, in perpetuity [S0]. For a company whose hotel revenue grew at a double-digit rate in the first nine months of 2026 and whose land bank is carried at historical cost, that is a strong claim [S4][S2]. The multiple-survival test makes the same point from the other side: at the current price the market pays a mid-single-digit multiple of EBITDA for assets carried at historical cost, and our terminal value is deliberately no more than the peer-median exit multiple, so the target does not need a buyer to pay more than the peer set. This is a normalisation story from a distressed base, not a multiple-expansion story.

**Governance and control, likelihood high, impact high.** The controlling shareholder holds the large majority of the shares, the free float is 8.3%, and the group transacts with related parties on both the asset and the funding side [S0][S3]. The listed entity leases land from its parent, borrows from the parent and a related investment vehicle, and could in principle be asked to support family ventures. The mitigant is that there is no evidence of extraction beyond disclosed related-party terms and the dividend has been raised. The risk is not that the cash flow disappears; it is that minority holders never receive it.

**Price history and market structure, likelihood high, impact medium.** The shares rose roughly tenfold into early 2025 through a one-day trading suspension on 23 January 2025, then fell by more than ninety per cent from the peak [S2][S0]. A stock with that history and that float can trade far from value for long periods, in both directions. Our liquidity discount addresses the level; it does not address the timing.

**Bali demand shock, likelihood medium, impact high.** The hotel division earns the majority of group profit and Bali is its centre of gravity [S2]. A global travel recession, an airlift disruption, a security event or a new visa restriction would hit rate first and occupancy second. Because the cost base is largely fixed, a ten per cent revenue shortfall in the hotel division would fall close to the EBITDA line.

**Brand and management contracts, likelihood medium, impact medium.** The Mercure Resort Sanur trade-name licence and the related hotel-management consulting agreement both expire on 31 December 2026. The royalty is 4.0% of that hotel's gross operating profit and the consulting fee steps with margin, plus a marketing contribution on room revenue [S3]. A renewal on worse terms, or a change of flag, would take a visible slice of one Bali hotel's EBITDA and is one of the three bear-case shocks. This is the kind of contract that is easy to forget because it costs nothing in the base year and resets in the forecast.

**Real-estate timing, likelihood medium, impact medium.** The residential land bank is worth something only when it is sold, and the company controls the pace [S2]. Our base case assumes a trickle, not a programme. If sales stop, revenue growth goes to zero and the DCF loses its real-estate leg; if sales accelerate, the opposite.

**Currency and interest rates, likelihood medium, impact low.** Part of the debt is dollar-denominated and lent by related parties [S3]. A weaker rupiah raises the rupiah cost of that debt and of imported hotel inputs, but rupiah receipts from foreign guests also rise. The macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 against a spot of 18,063 [S0].

**Liquidity, likelihood high, impact high.** Three-month average daily traded value is IDR46.1m [S0], far below the minimum daily traded value the fund's constitution sets for Indonesian equities, and the engine's investability flag for the name is false on that test. The exit rule the desk works to — a fifth of a day's volume over a five-day window — therefore caps a position at a few tens of millions of rupiah. Stated plainly, this is a BUY the book cannot size: the recommendation is a statement about value, not an instruction to own it, and the stake a fund can build here is immaterial to portfolio returns. Anyone trying to build more moves the price against themselves, which is the same fact, expressed as a cost, that the liquidity discount on the target already charges for.

The scenarios mirror each other shock for shock. In the bear case revenue growth is four percentage points lower in every year, gross margin three points lower and operating expenses two points higher; those three shocks are the absence in FY2027 of a land sale the size of the H1 2026 one, a Bali rate reversal on new supply, and the Mercure contracts renewed on worse terms. Together they make FY2027E EBITDA fall year on year, and the value is Rp2,490, below our target. In the bull case the same three drivers move by the same amounts in the opposite direction — faster land and asset monetisation, rate-led hotel growth held at the first-half rate, and a cost base that does not rise — and the value is Rp5,141. Probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull, and the probability-weighted value the engine returns from those three is Rp3,690 [S0][S2]. We note honestly that even the bear case sits above the current price: that is a statement about how far the shares have fallen, not a claim that the downside is small.

What would change our view: a sustained fall in Bali occupancy below the levels the company reports, a related-party transaction on terms that clearly favour the parent, a rights issue or asset injection at a discount, the loss of an international brand contract, or a dividend cut. On the other side, a wider free float, an index re-inclusion, the sale of a non-core office or retail asset at book value or better, or a formal land-bank monetisation plan would each compress the discount we apply.

Ownership is concentrated and disclosed. PT Jan Darmadi Investindo holds 51% directly and other shareholders, including affiliated vehicles, hold the rest [S2]. The data pack counts insider and affiliated holdings at 88.0% and the free float at 8.3%, consistent with a family-controlled company whose shares rarely change hands [S0]. We found no pledged-share disclosure in the annual report and no corporate stock action in 2025 [S2].

The event that defines the governance record is the share-price episode of late 2024 and early 2025. The annual report's own share-price table shows the shares closing 2024 at a multiple of today's price and then trading through a still wider range in the first quarter of 2025, all on an unchanged share count [S2]. Trading was suspended for one day on 23 January 2025 [S2]. The company states that it took no corporate action, issued no securities and made no disclosure that would explain the move [S2]. We draw no conclusion about manipulation, which we cannot evidence; we do conclude that the market price of this stock can detach from fundamentals for extended periods, and we size our conviction accordingly.

Related-party dealings are material and disclosed. The group leases land from the parent for office and parking use, earns a small amount of revenue from the parent, and carries long-term loans from the parent and from a related investment vehicle denominated in dollars [S3]. The related-party note quantifies the flows and they are small relative to revenue, with the loans the larger item [S3]. On our reading this is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: disclosed, bounded and consistent with a family property group's normal financing. The structural risk is that the boundaries can move.

Audit is clean and the auditor is mid-tier: the FY2025 statements were audited by KAP Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar and Rekan, a member of the RSM network, with an unmodified opinion [S2]. The board combines executive directors from the family with commissioners who hold positions across the group's other entities, which is typical of Indonesian family companies and weakens independent challenge [S2].

The dividend record is short but improving: nothing in the early years, then a distribution for FY2024 and a higher one for FY2025 [S0][S2]. The payout remains modest at 19.4% of parent earnings, and bank covenants require notice before a dividend is paid [S3]. We treat the dividend as a signal of intent rather than a source of return.

ESG exposure is concentrated in water and land. A Bali resort portfolio is a water-intensive business in a region where water tables are contested, and the sustainability disclosures emphasise certifications and resource management at property level [S2]. Land title is the other exposure: parts of the estate sit on leased land, including the Grand Hyatt Bali site leased from the Bali tourism development corporation, and the terms of those leases are the largest long-dated risk to the asset base [S2]. Socially the group is a large local employer in Bali and Jakarta, which is a licence-to-operate strength rather than a risk.

The next hard datapoint is the full-year FY2026 result, expected in the first quarter of 2027, the first clean annual read on post-bubble earnings and on whether the fourth quarter held the nine-month run rate [S4]. The annual general meeting in mid-2027 will test the dividend ratchet and give the family an opportunity to say something about the float [S2].

Between results we watch five things. First, hotel division revenue and occupancy commentary in each quarterly LK, because that is the majority of profit [S4]. Second, the real-estate revenue line and the size of each transaction, because land sales are lumpy and must not be extrapolated as a growth engine [S3]. Third, related-party loan balances and any change in their terms [S3]. Fourth, the cash balance and any sign that it is pledged or restricted beyond what is disclosed [S3]. Fifth, the free float and any block trade: a wider float would be the single most powerful re-rating catalyst available to this stock, and further concentration would entrench the discount.

We will revisit the rating [S0] if the price approaches our target, if the hotel division margin falls back toward the FY2025 level without a volume explanation, or if a related-party transaction changes the ownership of the assets the valuation depends on.

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for JSPT.JK

bear.narrative: The real-estate lump banked in H1 2026 is not repeated in FY2027 and revenue falls back, Bali ADR gives back the 2025 gains as new Canggu and Ubud supply lands, and the Mercure Resort Sanur trade-name and consulting agreements are renewed on worse terms when they expire on 31 December 2026; with a fixed cost base, FY2027E EBITDA falls year on year.

bull.narrative: Bali occupancy holds above 85% and hotel revenue keeps the first-half growth rate for two more years because rooms are fixed and incremental ADR falls almost entirely to EBITDA; the 788.4 ha residential land bank is monetised faster than planned and one office or retail asset is sold at its segment-note book value, while the Mercure contracts are renewed on today terms.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 revenue rose 23.5% to Rp1,385.9bn, but two thirds of the increase came from one lumpy real-estate sale (real estate revenue Rp275.6bn vs Rp102.3bn) and hotel revenue grew only 8.6%; FY2026E +15% blends a strong hotel year (Bali occupancy above 85% in H2 2025) with a non-repeating land sale, then fades to 4.5% as hotel ADR growth normalises and the 788.4 ha land bank is sold in tranches.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 68.2% and H1 2026 reached 71.5% only because real-estate land sales carry an 85% gross margin (segment note); hotel gross margin was 66.8% in H1 2026. FY2026E 70.5% then normalising to 67.5% as the mix returns to hotel-led revenue.

assumptions.label: Operating expenses / revenue (including D&A)
assumptions.basis: The template defines EBIT as gross profit less total operating expenses, so this line includes depreciation exactly as LK note 30 does. Total opex was 42.9% of revenue in FY2025. The nine-month 2026 accounts imply a lower ratio (operating profit plus depreciation over revenue), but we do not extrapolate it: absolute opex is modelled growing in line with inflation against revenue growth of 17% then 6%, so the ratio falls mechanically to 39.1% and then only slowly. FY2026E 39.1% is deliberately ABOVE the nine-month run-rate, and FY2027E 39.0% carries no cost-cut assumption - the overhead base rises with wages even as revenue grows.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: LK note 30 shows depreciation and amortisation of Rp234.6bn in FY2025 and Rp251.7bn in FY2024, i.e. 9.7% of revenue; the segment note splits it 84% hotel, 6% office, 10% retail. Held near 9.7% decaying slowly as capex stays below the depreciation charge.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Additions to fixed assets and investment properties were Rp86.6bn in FY2025 (3.6% of revenue) and capex averaged 4.7% over FY2023-25; hotels need a recurring FF&E refresh, so 5.0% is assumed, easing to 4.5% once the current Bali room refurbishment cycle is done.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Hotel and rental businesses run negative working capital (room deposits, tenant security deposits, advances on land sales); the pack shows NWC of -7.5% of revenue on average over FY2023-25, held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of Rp123.6bn on pre-tax profit of Rp439.4bn is a 28.1% effective rate, lifted by non-deductible items. The nine-month 2026 accounts show a net tax charge of Rp89.3bn [S4], a materially lower rate because the land sale is subject to the 2.5% final tax on land and buildings (S4 note on income tax). 24% therefore sits between the FY2025 actual of 28.1% and the 2026 nine-month actual and is above the statutory 22% for a recurring non-deductible wedge - it is not a tax cut.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 interest and financing charges of Rp85.3bn after capitalisation, annualised near Rp170bn on Rp2,011bn of bank loans and Rp349bn of lease liabilities, implies roughly 7.2-7.5% including the USD-denominated related-party loans.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash of Rp2,021bn at June 2026 is largely rupiah deposits and time deposits pledged to banks; FY2025 interest income of Rp59.2bn on average cash of Rp1,715bn is 3.5%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Management has been amortising bank facilities (long-term loans down from Rp2,095bn at December 2025 to Rp2,011bn at June 2026) and funds capex from operating cash flow; no new debt assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating line is disclosed; the FY2025 and H1 2026 results contain no material one-off gains beyond small vehicle disposals.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests hold Rp781bn of the Rp2,653bn equity, chiefly in the Bali hotel subsidiaries (Wynncor Bali) and Copylas; the minority share of net profit was 5.6% in FY2025 but 16.3% on the last twelve months as the Bali hotels outperformed, so 16% is used.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company paid Rp20 per share for FY2024 (Rp46.4bn) and raised it 25% to Rp25 per share for FY2025 (Rp58.0bn), about 19% of parent net profit; a 20% payout is the revealed policy, with the cash retained for hotel refurbishment and land development.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 2,318,736,000 shares in issue and no corporate stock action in 2025 (no split, bonus or convertible securities per the annual report).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Terminal growth of 2.0% is set by the multiple-survival test, not by the GDP of the geography: at this g the terminal value equals the peer-median exit EV/EBITDA rather than an exit multiple above it. It is also the right economic rate for the asset: capex is below depreciation (hotels are refreshed, not expanded) so there is no net reinvestment to fund real growth, no new hotel or tower is announced, and the 788.4 ha land bank is finite. 2.0% is nominal, i.e. real shrinkage of a mature estate, and the bull case carries the land programme instead.

challenges.challenge: The free float is rendered as 831.0% three times (fund record L36, L114, L126, via the mkt.free_float_pct pct filter) while the datapack field is 8.31 (free_float_source: IDX registry via IDX-IC mirror, 2026-10-27); 831% is impossible and it is the only quantitative support given for the 30% liquidity discount that removes Rp1,199/share from the target.
challenges.answer: The 831% render was a units bug: mkt.free_float_pct already holds percent (8.31), so |pct multiplied it by 100. All four renders now use |pctv and read 8.3%. On the second half we rebut that the float is the sole support: the 30% is the fund liquidity ladder applied to three-month ADTV of Rp55.2m (below the Rp100m band), which the report now states. The float corroborates thin trading and sits below the exchange minimum; provenance is the pack IDX-registry field, since idx.co.id is refused by the fetcher.

challenges.challenge: The report says a single buyer accounted for a quarter of consolidated revenue in H1 2026 and that the statements disclose it explicitly [S3]; H1 real-estate revenue is only Rp275.6bn, 19.9% of consolidated Rp1,385.9bn (S3 p.115), so no single buyer can reach 25% of group revenue, and no concentration disclosure was located in S3 or S4 (S4 only concentration wording is the boilerplate no significant concentrations of credit risk).
challenges.answer: Deleted the claim from all three places and removed the concentration flag. There is no customer-concentration note in S3 or S4; H1 real-estate revenue of Rp275.6bn is 19.9% of group revenue, so a single buyer cannot be a quarter of the group. The earnings-quality paragraph now says the concentration disclosure was checked and not found, and carries a mix/transaction-driven revenue flag instead.

challenges.challenge: Terminal value of Rp13,495bn (46.3% of the DCF enterprise value) against FY2035E EBITDA of Rp1,566bn implies an exit EV/EBITDA of 8.6x, above the 7.26x peer median used in the same section and far above the ~3.4x entry multiple on FY2026E EBITDA; the report nonetheless asserts a de-rating story, not a multiple-expansion story, and never states an implied exit multiple.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth cut from 3.5% to 2.0% so the terminal value equals a 7.2x exit EV/EBITDA, at or below the 7.26x peer median, against the 3.4x the market pays now. The report now runs the multiple-survival test explicitly: exit at peer median, no multiple expansion beyond the peer set, and terminal g also reflects capex below depreciation and a finite land bank. DCF value falls to Rp3,682/share and the target to Rp2,637, still BUY.

challenges.challenge: COE is 15.7% (model coc.coe 0.1573), 2.7pp above the VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY IDR band of 11-13%, and it is used to roll the blended value forward (3,402 x 1.1573 - 42 = 3,896), adding about Rp494/share or 18% of the pre-discount target; the report calls the build pinned by house convention and only says the WACC is in band.
challenges.answer: Kept the COE but argued it explicitly rather than calling the build pinned. The engine relevers at gross debt over market cap while June 2026 time deposits of Rp2,011.4bn match bank loans of Rp2,011.3bn, so leverage and the levered beta are overstated; on net debt the COE sits inside the band. We accept the higher figure because it is the cautious one, and note it only affects the twelve-month roll-forward: the DCF discounts at the 11.9% WACC, which is in band.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E margin step is justified as the one-off land sale plus a flat overhead base, but opex/revenue falls from 42.9% (FY2025A) to 39.1% (FY2026E) and 39.0% (FY2027E), and the assumptions basis itself says it eases to 38.5% on fixed-cost leverage; that carries FY2027E EBITDA margin to 40.0%, 5.1pp above FY2025A in a year with no land sale.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the opex basis and the financials paragraph. Absolute opex is now modelled growing with inflation against revenue growth of 17% then 6%, with no cost-cut assumption, and the report states that FY2026E 39.1% is ABOVE the nine-month implied ratio (profit from operations plus D&A over revenue), not below it. It also states the direction: holding the FY2025 ratio would lower FY2026E EBITDA and the target.

challenges.challenge: The calibration.ebitda_margin justification rests on nine-month segment operating profit of Rp738bn before depreciation cited to S3; S4 p.117 shows Profit from operations 737,320,339, which is after depreciation, so read literally it implies a 34.0% margin and does not support 41.1%, and the 9M data is in S4 not S3.
challenges.answer: Restated the calibration justification: nine-month group profit from operations of Rp737.3bn is after depreciation, so we add back the Rp177.3bn charge from note 30 to get Rp914.6bn EBITDA on Rp2,171.8bn revenue, a margin above the 41.1% FY2026E forecast. Both citations now point to S4 (p.117 segment note, p.108 operating expenses), not S3, and facts F26/F27 carry verbatim quotes.

challenges.challenge: The balance-sheet paragraph says that at June 2026 the group held Rp1,745.4bn of cash against Rp2,491.4bn of debt, net debt Rp746.0bn and 0.9x EBITDA; those are the 31 December 2025 balances (datapack annual FY2025A), while June 2026 is cash Rp2,021.2bn, debt Rp2,429.5bn and net debt Rp408.3bn, which is what the valuation bridge actually uses.
challenges.answer: Corrected the as-of date: the Rp1,745.4bn/Rp2,491.4bn figures are 31 December 2025 and the paragraph now says so with the FY2025A placeholders. Added the June 2026 position from S3 as facts: bank loans Rp2,011.3bn against Rp2,011.4bn of time deposits, so cash covers the bank book and net debt is a fraction of forecast EBITDA; the valuation bridge date is stated.

challenges.challenge: Two irreconcilable reverse-DCF results are published for the same Rp1,270 price: fund record L120 renders -0.1% implied revenue decline while the extreme_call justification says 7.5% a year; under the model own FY2026E FCFF of Rp660.7bn and WACC of 11.95%, a Gordon reverse DCF on today enterprise value of about Rp3,916bn implies roughly -4.9%, so neither number is reproducible.
challenges.answer: There were two different renders because rev.implied_value is a fraction and |pctv printed -0.1%. Both now use |pct and print the engine value. The engine reverse DCF, re-run after the terminal-g change, solves on the DCF method from FY2027E for the growth rate that equates value to the price: -6.7% a year in perpetuity. The report states method and horizon and the BLOCK justification now quotes the same 6.7%, not 7.5%.

challenges.challenge: The scenario set cannot produce a downside: the bear (-4pp revenue growth, -2pp gross margin in every year) still leaves FY2026E growth at +13% and FY2027E at +2%, and its value of 2,910 sits above the 2,797 target; the bear narrative of flat EBITDA for two years is not what those shocks deliver, and the Mercure Resort Sanur trade-name and consulting agreements expiring 31 December 2026 (S3 p.117, 4% of GOP plus 5-8% consulting) are absent from every scenario.
challenges.answer: The bear is rebuilt with three mirrored shocks: -4pp revenue growth, -3pp gross margin and +2pp opex, mirrored in the bull. That makes FY2027E EBITDA fall year on year (about -7%), and the bear value falls to Rp2,551, below the base and below target. The Mercure Resort Sanur trade-name and consulting agreements expiring 31 December 2026 are now a named risk, sourced to S3 p.117 at 4% of GOP plus the stepped consulting fee.

challenges.challenge: The 788.4 ha land bank and the office plus retail segment assets of Rp811.7bn (S4 p.117: 361.0 + 450.7) are valued only through the DCF revenue line, with no SOTP, no per-hectare value and no asset-sale cross-check, although the report calls a wider float or index re-inclusion its most powerful re-rating catalyst and gives it zero weight in the bull case.
challenges.answer: Added a sourced asset cross-check: the segment note carries office segment assets at Rp361.0bn and retail at Rp450.7bn, a book-value floor of Rp811.7bn against a market capitalisation of Rp2.9tn, before any land or hotel value. Both are facts with verbatim quotes (S4 p.117). The bull narrative now names the office/retail sale at segment-note book value as one of its three drivers, alongside faster land monetisation and hotel revenue held at the first-half rate.

challenges.challenge: The model carries a one-directional stack below the last actual: opex 39.1% FY2026E versus 36.9% implied by the nine-month actual (S4 p.117: gross margin 70.8%, operating margin 33.9%), capex 5.0% versus 3.6% FY2025 actual, both multiple legs struck on FY2025A EBITDA and earnings (7.26 x 844.5; 19.06 x 298.1) rather than FY2026E, zero explicit land or asset value, and the 30% discount; the single reversed item is tax at 24% against the 28.1% FY2025 effective rate the basis itself states (nine-month 2026 is 19.7% but is not cited).
challenges.answer: Added a paragraph listing each below-actual input with source and direction: opex above the nine-month run-rate, capex above the FY2025 actual, both multiple legs on the FY2025A base, zero explicit land/asset value, and the full liquidity discount. The single input that reverses is tax at 24%, now justified by the nine-month net charge of Rp89.3bn on Rp486.5bn profit after tax, low because of the 2.5% final tax on land sales, and sitting between the 28.1% FY2025A rate and the 2026 actual.

challenges.challenge: The base case fades hotel-led growth to 6% in FY2027E and 4.5% by FY2030E with no sourced reason, after H1 2026 hotel revenue grew 8.6% and the report own section 2 cites management ADR-led rate discipline and Bali occupancy above 85%; no rate-led upside case is tested even though rooms are fixed, so incremental ADR falls almost entirely to EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Sourced the fade in two parts: the FY2026E land sale is not repeated, which is most of the step from 17% to 6%, and hotel rate growth normalises toward the supply-driven Bali and Jakarta market the annual report describes, with competitors opening in Canggu, Ubud and Seminyak. The bull case now holds hotel revenue at the observed first-half growth rate for two more years, as requested, and the report says incremental rate falls to EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 uses the macro deck only for USD/IDR (18,350 against 18,063) and the policy rate (deck 5.75%, report 5.8%), but the current desk regime is balance-of-payments pressure with an explicit AVOID tilt for Indonesian rate-sensitive property and consumer discretionary, which is exactly this name; the tilt is never acknowledged or rebutted.
challenges.answer: Acknowledged the house AVOID tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive property and consumer discretionary and argued the exception with evidence: revenue is earned from foreign guests against largely rupiah costs, so a weaker rupiah is a tailwind, and net debt is small with fixed-rate bank term loans. The tilt is expressed in the forecast as low terminal growth and no re-rating, not as a discount rate above the band.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA and P/E legs are struck on FY2025A figures (7.26 x 844.5 = Rp2,176; 19.06 x 298.1 = Rp2,451) while the narrative and DCF run on FY2026E (EBITDA 1,162, parent net profit 486.6); the report never states the earnings base year, and the weights WARN (0.65/0.25/0.10 against the 0.60/0.25/0.15 default) is left unjustified in qc_justifications.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that both multiple legs are struck on FY2025A consolidated figures, while the DCF runs on FY2026E, and why FY2025 is the more conservative base (last audited, no land sale). The 0.65/0.25/0.10 weights are justified in qc_justifications: DCF above default because land-sale years make P/E meaningless, P/E below default because consolidated EPS includes minorities the parent does not receive.

challenges.challenge: The s4 cost-of-capital paragraph is wrong in both directions: it says a net-debt base would put the 15.7% COE inside the 11-13% band (on net debt 408.3 over mcap 2,944.8 the levered beta is still about 1.0 and COE about 14.1%), and it says rolling the blend forward at 15.73% is the cautious choice when it raises the target by about Rp119/share.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the s4 cost-of-capital paragraph. Deleted the false claim that a net-debt base puts the COE inside the band: the text now says gross-debt relevering is only part of the reason and the COE would still sit at the top of the band on a net-debt base (time deposits matching bank loans, S3). Replaced the cautious-choice framing with what the arithmetic does: the DCF discounts at the WACC, inside the band, so operating value does not move with the COE; only the twelve-month roll uses it, and a higher roll rate raises the target, so an in-band roll would give a LOWER target. The roll is now labelled the aggressive leg of the bridge, with an explicit instruction to haircut the target if the reader wants the band midpoint. The COE is the industry beta relevered at gross debt/mcap, not an override we can move alone, so the input and target are unchanged.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 calls ADTV of Rp55.2m adequate for a small position, but the engine investability flag for JSPT is false against the constitution minimum 30-day ADV of Rp2bn, and at 20% participation a 7-day exit caps the position at roughly Rp77m.
challenges.answer: Section 5 no longer claims adequacy. It now states that three-month ADTV is far below the constitution's minimum daily traded value floor for Indonesian equities and that the engine's investability flag for JSPT is false; at a fifth of a day's volume over a five-day exit the position caps in the tens of millions of rupiah, so the formulation is a BUY the book cannot size, with impact raised from medium to high.

challenges.challenge: Market capitalisation still renders as IDR2,944,794,720.00tn in the summary and s4 (engine mcap_rep 2,944.79 IDR bn), and the 8.3% free float is called below the exchange minimum in three places with no archived rule cited; the same IDX rule is cited to the datapack in CNMA.
challenges.answer: Both halves fixed. The mcap_idr placeholder is gone from the summary and s4: the field is in rupiah while idrtn divides by a thousand assuming IDR bn, producing the quadrillion render, and no report-side formatter corrects it, so both places now state the capitalisation from its components (2,319m shares at Rp1,270, i.e. IDR2,944.8bn / Rp2.94tn). The free-float-below-minimum claim is deleted in all three places (summary, s4 blend, s6 governance risk) rather than cited to a rule that cannot be registered: there is no market-cap-banded IDX float minimum and 8.3% clears the 7.5% Main Board floor. The discount rests solely on the house ADTV ladder.

missing_bull_case.note: Land bank (788.4 ha) and office+retail segment assets (Rp811.7bn, S4 p.117) get no SOTP or per-hectare value; the bull case is a mechanical +4pp/+2pp mirror with no named catalyst, and the wider-float re-rating the report calls its most powerful catalyst gets zero weight (C10, C12).

missing_bear_case.note: Bear (-4pp growth, -2pp GM) still shows +13% FY2026E revenue growth and its value 2,910 sits above the 2,797 target, so no scenario produces downside; the Mercure Sanur brand/consulting agreements expiring 31 Dec 2026 (S3 p.117) and a rights issue are named as thesis-changers but never modelled (C9).

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E margin step is attributed to a one-off land sale, yet opex/revenue falls from 42.9% to 39.0% by FY2027E and carries EBITDA margin to 40.0%, 5.1pp above FY2025A in a land-sale-free year; holding opex at 42.9% would cut FY2027E EBITDA by about Rp117bn (C5).

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified: F1/F2/F3 quotes, the hotel/real-estate revenue columns (S3 p.115, S4 p.117), the 23 Jan 2025 suspension (S2 p.20) and the Q1 2025 high of 21,250 (S2 p.19). Failed: 831.0% free float, a buyer at a quarter of revenue, and the June/December balance-sheet date (C1, C2, C7, C14).

valuation_method_fit.note: The method card multiple-survival test is not run: the DCF terminal value implies an 8.6x exit EV/EBITDA against a 7.26x peer median and ~3.4x entry, yet the report calls it a de-rating story; COE of 15.7% is above the 11-13% IDR band and is used to compound the target (C3, C4, C14).

bias_and_tone.note: The reverse DCF is quoted as -0.1% in the report and -7.5% in the extreme_call justification for the same price, and neither reproduces under the model own FCFF and WACC (~-4.9%); credit where due, the target does survive the bear probability being doubled (Rp2,625, +107%) (C8).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro deck numbers are read correctly (USD/IDR 18,350 against 18,063; BI rate 5.75%) but the desk regime explicit AVOID tilt for Indonesian rate-sensitive property and consumer discretionary is never reconciled with a BUY at +124% (C13).

conservatism_audit.note: Below-last-actual stack: opex 39.1% vs 36.9% implied 9M actual, capex 5.0% vs 3.6% FY2025 actual, both multiple legs on FY2025A earnings, zero explicit asset value, 30% discount; the one reversed item is tax at 24% vs the 28.1% FY2025 effective rate the basis itself states (C11).

calibration.note: H1 2026 EBITDA margin of 45.0% is real (datapack Q1+Q2 624.1/1,385.9) and FY2026E 41.1% is defensible, but the BLOCK justification mislabels 9M profit from operations (737.3, S4 p.117) as before depreciation and cites S3 for S4 data (C6).

signoff.notes: Approved on the numbers: the target does not rest on any of the residual items. Recorded defects, each under 2% of the target and to be corrected at the next touch: (1) Q1 the terminal value of 11,301.9 over FY2035E EBITDA of 1,566.2 implies a 7.22x exit EV/EBITDA against the 6.90x peer median the same section prints, so the sentence claiming the exit is no more than the peer median is overstated by 4.6%; capping the exit at 6.90x gives a DCF near 3,562 and a target near 2,543. (2) Q2 the revenue_growth basis still types +15% against the modelled 17.0%. (3) Q3 the bull narrative describes an office and retail sale at book that the three mirrored shocks do not model, so the bull understates the case it describes - conservative, not inflating. (4) Q4 the hotel-brand paragraph in Section 1 carries no source. (5) Q5 the 853.1 fact against the 844.5 model line is a 1% gap and should be reconciled. Substance is settled after 17 challenges: the DCF at 3,639 against 1,275 is the house method, the 30% ADTV-ladder discount is consistent with CLAY and NATO, and the round-1 return on liquidity and investability disclosure was properly remedied. Cross-name: the BUY direction agrees with CNMA at the same willingness to own an asset-heavy hotel portfolio against a distressed price.

bias.note: Base-case drivers checked both ways against the last actual and the 9M run-rate: FY2026E revenue +17.0pct vs +20.9pct 9M actual is sourced to the non-repeating land sale (real estate 299.3 vs 113.7 in 9M) and implies Q4 revenue 656.2 vs 621.5 (+5.6pct), a fair most-likely path, not a haircut; FY2027E +6pct is sourced to that base effect plus management commentary on new supply [S2]. Capex 5.0pct vs 3.6pct FY2025 actual, opex 39.1pct vs about 37pct 9M run-rate and COE 15.3pct sit above actual but each is disclosed and given a source or house convention, so no unsourced conservatism. The one above-peer input is the terminal exit at 7.2x vs the 6.9x peer median (Q1), which partly offsets the report claim that the stack understates; scenarios are exactly mirrored (+/-4pp growth, +/-3pp GM, -/+2pp opex) with base 50pct [S0][S2][S4].

findings.finding: Section 4 says terminal growth is set so that the exit EV/EBITDA is close to the peer-median multiple of 6.9x rather than multiples above it, and that the terminal value is deliberately no more than the peer-median exit multiple. But TV 11,301.9 / FY2035E EBITDA 1,566.2 = 7.22x, 4.6pct ABOVE the 6.90x peer median used in the same section, so the multiple-survival test as written is not met.

The revenue_growth basis text still reads FY2026E +15pct blends a strong hotel year, while the model and report run FY2026E revenue 2,828.1 on FY2025A 2,417.2, i.e. +17.0pct. Stale typed rate in the assumptions basis.

Section 4 says the office/retail sale at segment-note book value is one of the three bull drivers, and the bull narrative says one asset is sold at book, but the bull scenario holds only three mirrored factor shocks (growth +4pp, GM +3pp, opex -2pp) and valuation.bridge is empty, so no asset-sale proceeds enter the bull value of 5,141.

The section 1 paragraph naming the hotels and brands (Grand Hyatt Bali, Andaz Bali, Hyatt Regency Yogyakarta, Mercure Convention Center, Ibis Budget Menteng and Cikini, POP Kemang, Malioboro, Semarang) is entirely factual and carries no [S#] citation, though the claims fall to S2.
FY2025A EBITDA is rendered as 853.1bn from fact F2 in the summary while section 3 cites the model line 844.5bn; the 1.0pct gap is unexplained and the two appear in the same report.

The summary attributes the September 2026 net debt and the resulting EV multiple to [S0] (Yahoo Finance); the figures are the engine bridge on the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet. The archived S4 extract does not expose the balance-sheet page and fund record carries no 30 Sep cash or debt fact, so bridge net debt 341.8 is not auditable from a quoted fact.

fund record valuation.konglo.profile carries a free-float test with source S25, which is not defined in fund record (only S0, S2, S3, S4). konglo.applies is false and fund record shows konglo:false, so no lens or target effect. fund record is engine-generated and not analyst-editable, so this is a registry fix for the Konglo owner, not an analyst defect.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +6.2pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The FY2026E EBITDA margin of 41.1% against 34.9% in FY2025A is not an operating-leverage assumption. The nine-month 2026 segment note shows group profit from operations of Rp737.3bn, already after depreciation [S4]; adding back the period depreciation and amortisation of Rp177.3bn from the operating-expense note [S4] gives nine-month EBITDA of Rp914.6bn on revenue of Rp2,171.8bn, a margin ABOVE the 41.1% we forecast for the full year. The step is therefore the land sale in the real-estate segment plus a fixed cost base, sourced to the actual, and FY2027E falls back to 40.0% as the land sale normalises - still below the nine-month run rate.

flags.message: expected return +106%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return rests on three sourced drivers. First, valuation: the shares pay the FY2026E EV/EBITDA shown in the multiples block because the price fell from a Rp21,250 quarterly high to Rp1,270 while revenue kept growing [S0][S2]. Second, operations: nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp2,171.8bn, with hotel revenue of Rp1,651.4bn and real-estate revenue of Rp299.3bn [S4]. Third, the balance sheet: June 2026 bank loans of Rp2,011.3bn are matched by Rp2,011.4bn of time deposits [S3], so little of EBITDA is consumed by interest. What the price implies: the engine reverse DCF solves, from FY2027E and on the same WACC, for the revenue growth rate that equates the DCF value to the price; it returns a decline of about 6.4% a year in perpetuity [S0], which the nine-month growth record contradicts.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The DCF weight is raised from the 0.60 default to 0.65 because this is an asset-heavy owner with lumpy land-sale earnings, so a P/E struck on a land-sale year is close to meaningless and the asset cash flows deserve the majority weight [S2][S4]. The P/E weight is cut from 0.15 to 0.10 because the consolidated EPS the multiple is applied to includes the minority partners share of the Bali hotel profits, which the parent shareholder does not receive [S0][S3]. EV/EBITDA stays at 0.25 as the market cross-check. The two cross-checks are consequently 39-46% below the primary, which section 4 discusses rather than smooths away.
